detail.abstract: Every 10 November at 09:05 sirens sound across Turkey for Atatürk, and many drivers stop their vehicles on the road. We ask how much this slows Istanbul's traffic. We use the municipality's open data on hourly speeds in about 2 305 one-kilometre cells for 2020-2024. For each cell we compare the 09:00 hour with the hours before and after it, and we compare 10 November with 74 other dates of the same weekday in the surrounding sixteen weeks. Significance is judged against all 983 040 ways of picking one date per year as the event. Across all cells the 09:00 hour was slower on 10 November by the equivalent of 0.18 minutes of full stop per vehicle (p = 0.116), which is not distinguishable from an ordinary date. In cells that normally flow at 50-70 km/h the 09:00 hour lay below the line between its neighbours in all five years, by the equivalent of 0.64 minutes (90% interval 0.26 to 1.05; p = 0.003, and 0.015 after adjustment for testing four speed classes). Part of this gap arises because the 10:00 hour was unusually fast on 10 November. Against hours that do not adjoin the siren, the 09:00 hour was slower by 0.43 minutes (p = 0.101). The lowest recorded speed in the hour fell by 4.7%, while the highest speed and the number of vehicles did not change. On slow streets, cells in neighbourhoods with a higher vote for the CHP slowed more at 09:00 in all five years (p = 0.0007). The data contain no stationary vehicles, so these figures bound the true delay from below.

detail.abstract: Views are among the most valued and least measured attributes of a home. We present an open-data method that estimates the sea-view potential of every free façade of every residential building at three floors (ground, middle and top; other floors take the nearest of them), from cadastral footprints with floor counts and a national terrain model. Run for 158,060 buildings of 21 municipalities on Spain's Costa del Sol in under an hour on two cores, it finds that 52 % of buildings see some sea from their top floor and 36 % have an open view (20° or more). Traced over a LiDAR surface in a pilot, scores agree with the model's inside cadastral footprints (96.7 % of viewpoints in the same class at 20°), but structures the cadastre does not record lower the sea seen from the top floor by 6.1–9.0° on average. Against the photographs of 93 homes for sale, labelled blind by AI models of two developers with ties decided by the author, the score has an AUC of 0.80 (95 % CI 0.70–0.89; 0.81 against the first-round labels); at 20° it is sensitive (0.90) but not specific (0.45). Dwelling figures depend on how dwellings are allocated to façades and floors: 42 % of dwellings are on a floor with open-view potential under the main rule, and 12–45 % across the allocation, geometry and vegetation scenarios tested. As an application, higher-income census sections tend to have more modelled view potential within municipalities, with uncertain size and fragile inference (about two effective clusters); on terrain alone the difference largely disappears. Code and façade-level data reproduce the main results. CASAS.ES also publishes the article and its methodology.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces Four-Point Verification, an instrument for testing the trustworthiness of a legal reference at a moment when machines help draft it. Every reference is examined at four points — wording, number, status, and tempus — which fall into two layers: whether the reference exists, and whether what exists is true in the case at hand. Its distinctive features are a two-legged temporal gate, the time of the act and the time of adjudication, and the rotation of the four points into the body of civil-law judgments rather than only into the document about to be filed. The paper frames the instrument as a doctrine of validity conditions for references, parallel in logic to the civil-law doctrine of the conditions for a valid contract, and as the floor of a standard of examinability. Its originality claim is narrowed openly against two earlier comparators, supported by a prior-art search registered in advance.

detail.abstract: The UK budget of 28th October 2026 announced a one-off £100 Household Energy Payment for homes in council tax bands A to D in England, and the abolition of the standing charge on domestic gas bills. We assess both measures using official open data and fully reproducible code. A microsimulation on 4,000,000 anonymised household records from the National Energy Efficiency Data-Framework, updated to 2024 consumption, is combined with meter data for all 33,755 English neighbourhoods, a degree-day model of heat demand and local insolvency statistics. Recovering the £108 standing charge through the unit rate adds 0.95p per kWh and leaves a bill unchanged at 11,359 kWh a year. We find that 59% of homes with gas pay less, by £43 a year on average, while 41% pay £57 more. Gains are concentrated in deprived areas, flats and small homes. The payment reaches 99% of homes in the most deprived tenth of neighbourhoods and about 84% of fuel-poor households, yet only about a tenth of its cost goes to fuel-poor households. Set against bills without the measures, 45% of English homes gain from both in 2027, and 11% receive no payment and pay more for gas. Net gains are strongly associated with local personal insolvency rates (rank correlation 0.76). The reform changes the seasonal shape and weather sensitivity of household bills only modestly, but it exposes about £2.7 billion of supplier revenue to the weather. The share of winners falls to 46% if the new unit rate is set at Ofgem's typical consumption value instead of mean consumption. Both measures arrive as prices rise. Forecasts published in early November 2026 put the price cap for January to March 2027 at about £2,187 for a typical home, 27% above today's, with a further small rise in April before prices ease from July. On that path the average English home pays £448 more for energy in 2027 than at today's prices. The two measures offset 28% of the increase in the most deprived fifth of neighbourhoods and 8% in the least deprived. The price rise does not change who gains from the standing charge reform.
